finding.claim: Mass assignment on PUT /me: any key in the request body is copied onto the persisted user record, so an authenticated user can set privilege or identity fields (role, isAdmin, permissions, emailVerified, email, password hash, id) on their own account.
finding.source: req.body of PUT /me (HTTP client, authenticated as any user; body is attacker-controlled).
finding.sink: Object.assign(req.user, req.body) at users.js:5, persisted by req.store.save(req.user) at users.js:6.

trace.note: Route handler for PUT /me; no field validation or auth check in this file.
Object.assign copies every own enumerable key of req.body onto req.user.
req.store.save persists the mutated user object with the injected fields.
Updated user, including injected fields, is returned to the client.

finding.guards_checked: No allowlist, schema, or field filter in users.js. The sibling handler at users.js:11-12 allowlists displayName and bio, which shows the intended control was not applied here. Upstream body parser, auth middleware, and store behavior are not in the repo, so actual impact depends on the user schema (unverified). Severity rises if the schema has privilege fields.

verdict.guard_found: none. users.js:4-7 has no field allowlist, schema, or auth check. The sibling handler at users.js:11-12 allowlists displayName and bio, so the protection exists only on /me/profile. The upstream body parser, auth middleware, and store are not in the repo.
verdict.reason: The trace matches users.js:4-7: Object.assign at line 5 copies every key of req.body onto req.user, and req.store.save at line 6 persists it, with no effective control in the repo. The mass-assignment defect is confirmed, but the privilege-escalation impact depends on the user schema, which is not in the repo and remains unverified.

finding.claim: If req.store.save upserts by primary key, a request body containing another user's id overwrites that user's record (cross-account write).
finding.sink: Object.assign at users.js:5 changes req.user.id, then req.store.save at users.js:6 writes the record keyed by that id.

trace.note: Body key id overwrites req.user.id with a victim's id.
save(req.user) is keyed by the mutated id, so the victim record would be replaced with the attacker's data.

finding.guards_checked: No check that id is immutable or matches the session user. Whether save keys by id is unknown because store code is not in the repo. Conditional on the store implementation; confidence is low until that is verified.

verdict.guard_found: none in users.js. Nothing between the request and the effect: users.js:5 Object.assign(req.user, req.body) copies every body key, including id, and users.js:6 req.store.save(req.user) is a bare call whose result is unused. The auth middleware and req.store implementation are not in the repo (Glob of the directory returns only users.js), so any guard there is unknown.
verdict.reason: users.js:5 does copy req.body.id onto req.user and users.js:6 saves req.user, so the trace is accurate, but whether this overwrites another account depends on req.store.save (not in the repo) keying on id and on req.user being a per-user store record rather than a session object, so the cross-account write can be neither confirmed nor refuted from this code.

finding.claim: A JSON body with an own key '__proto__' changes the prototype of req.user for the rest of the request, so inherited properties (for example, isAdmin) can appear on the user object.
finding.source: req.body with key "__proto__" in PUT /me (attacker-controlled JSON).
finding.sink: Object.assign at users.js:5 uses [[Set]] for the key, which invokes the Object.prototype.__proto__ setter on req.user. Effect is on that object only, not global Object.prototype, because Object.assign is not recursive.

trace.note: Object.assign iterates own keys of req.body; key __proto__ triggers the inherited setter on req.user, replacing its prototype with the attacker object.
save(req.user) may serialize inherited properties if the store uses for-in or spread, which would persist them.
JSON serialization uses own properties, so the response itself does not show inherited values.

finding.guards_checked: No key filtering. Prototype-swap impact depends on whether later checks read inherited properties and whether store.save serializes them. Global pollution is not reachable from this code path. Confidence low to medium.

verdict.guard_found: none. No key filtering at users.js:5, and the handler is reachable only by an authenticated user since it operates on req.user. The prototype swap is the only effect and it does not add power.
verdict.reason: The trace is accurate: Object.assign at users.js:5 does [[Set]] on the __proto__ key and so swaps the prototype of req.user. But the attacker is an authenticated user acting on their own object, and users.js:5 copies arbitrary own keys with no filter, so they can already set isAdmin directly as an own property. An inherited isAdmin therefore grants nothing new, and no cross-user or global impact is shown in users.js.

finding.claim: Partial update erases profile fields: a PUT /me/profile request that omits bio (or displayName) sets that field to undefined on the user record, so the stored value is lost.
finding.source: req.body.displayName / req.body.bio in PUT /me/profile (client-controlled, may be omitted).
finding.sink: Object.assign(req.user, { displayName, bio }) at users.js:12 followed by req.store.save at users.js:13.

trace.note: Destructures displayName and bio from req.body; missing keys become undefined.
Object.assign copies undefined values, so existing fields are overwritten with undefined.

finding.guards_checked: No check for undefined or for merge semantics. This is a logic flaw (data loss), not a privilege issue. Impact depends on how the store serializes undefined.

verdict.guard_found: none. No guard sits between the caller and the write at users.js:11-13. The trace is accurate: users.js:11 destructures the keys, users.js:12 Object.assign copies undefined values, and users.js:13 saves. The attacker must be an authenticated user, and the write only touches req.user, which is the caller's own record. Nothing in the directory shows the auth middleware that sets req.user, so I am assuming it is the caller's own record.
verdict.reason: The trace at users.js:11-13 is accurate, but the effect is limited to the caller's own profile (users.js:12 writes req.user, set by middleware not included here), so it is a self-inflicted data-loss logic bug, not a security vulnerability; the candidate's own note concedes it is "not a privilege issue."

finding.claim: displayName and bio are accepted without type or length checks, so non-string values (objects, arrays) and unbounded strings are persisted.
finding.sink: Object.assign at users.js:12 followed by req.store.save at users.js:13 and response at users.js:14.

trace.note: Values are destructured with no type check.
Values are copied onto the stored user object unchanged.

finding.guards_checked: No validation in this file. If the store is a document database that interprets object keys starting with $, stored objects could alter queries later (not verifiable here). Unbounded length may also be a storage or resource issue. Confidence low.

verdict.guard_found: none. users.js:11 destructures req.body with no type or length check, users.js:12 copies the values onto req.user via Object.assign, and users.js:13 passes them to req.store.save unchanged. No validation middleware or schema exists in the directory (grep finds no other matches).
verdict.reason: The trace matches users.js:11-14 exactly, and the attacker is any user who reaches PUT /me/profile and can only write their own req.user record (auth middleware is not in this directory, so that is assumed). Non-string values and unbounded strings are persisted at users.js:12-13, so the stated claim holds; its security impact (for example NoSQL $-key operator injection) depends on the unseen store and is not demonstrated, so severity is low.

finding.claim: save() is not awaited and the response is sent before persistence is confirmed, so a failed save is reported to the client as success.
finding.source: Any failure from req.store.save (storage error, validation error in the store).
finding.sink: Client response at users.js:7 and users.js:14 claims success before the write completes.

trace.note: save is called without await or a callback; if it returns a promise, rejection is unhandled.
res.json sends success regardless of persistence outcome.

finding.guards_checked: Whether save is synchronous or async is not visible in the repo. If it is async, this is an error-handling and integrity flaw; if synchronous, it is not an issue. Confidence low until the store is read.

verdict.guard_found: none. users.js:6 and users.js:13 call req.store.save with no await, callback, or result check, and users.js:7 and users.js:14 send res.json unconditionally. No try/catch or error middleware is visible in users.js. The directory contains only users.js, so the store implementation and any app-level error handler are not available.
verdict.reason: The trace lines at users.js:6-7 and 13-14 match the candidate's description, but whether a failed save reaches the client as success depends on whether req.store.save is async, which cannot be determined because the store module is not in the repo; the attacker would be an authenticated user writing their own record, so this is an integrity/error-reporting issue rather than a privilege issue.

finding.claim: The full user object is returned to the client after update; if req.user contains secrets (password hash, tokens, API keys), they are disclosed.
finding.source: req.user contents, loaded upstream (not visible here).

trace.note: Serializes the entire req.user object back to the caller.
Same full-object response on the profile route.

finding.guards_checked: No projection or field exclusion in this file. Whether req.user holds secrets depends on the upstream loader, which is not in the repo. Conditional, low confidence.

verdict.guard_found: none. No field projection or exclusion exists in users.js. The only handling is Object.assign(req.user, ...) at users.js:5 and users.js:12, which writes without filtering the response, and res.json(req.user) at users.js:7 and users.js:14 returns the whole object.
verdict.reason: Both sinks at users.js:7 and users.js:14 do serialize the full req.user, but whether that exposes secrets depends on the upstream loader that populates req.user, which is not in the repo, and the caller is the user's own account (the /me routes), so this is UNVERIFIABLE rather than CONFIRMED.
